summary: A group of people your work is meant to help.
example: Depot staff, whom the Quality Check Rollout is meant to help.
definition: A group of people your projects, programmes or operations are meant to help. It says who they are, not how many. It is not a segment (a part you compare numbers across), not a stakeholder (someone with a say in the work), not a single person, and not the team or role doing the work.

/metadata/name.guide: A short plural name for the group, in the words your organisation uses.

poor.why: Leave the count out. The name says who; numbers come from a data source.
A benefit, not a group. Name the people who get it.
A role that does the work, not people the work helps. Add it as a resource.

/spec/description.guide: Who is in the group and who is not, in one sentence without numbers.
good: Members who deliver produce to a depot during the season.
Workers hired by members for harvest and delivery during the peak months.

poor.why: Repeats the name and does not say who is in or out: every member, or only those who deliver?

poor.text: Everyone who benefits from the cooperative.
poor.why: Too broad to sort anyone by, and it describes a benefit rather than a group.

/spec/source.guide: The data source that lists the people in this group. Leave it empty if none does.

poor.why: It records collections, not who is in the group.

Project:/spec/summary/beneficiaries/-/gr.ask: Which projects are meant to help this group?
Project:/spec/summary/beneficiaries/-/gr.ifNone: None yet is fine. A project names this group when it is meant to help them.

Programme:/spec/problems/-/groups/-.ask: Which programme problems affect this group?
Programme:/spec/problems/-/groups/-.ifNone: None yet is fine. A programme names this group on each problem that affects them.
